cases.name: unresolved-status-collision
cases.trap: Choose an authoritative definition for completed from contradictory documents without an accepted decision.
cases.prompt: Two documents in the same workflow domain disagree. An engineering runbook says `completed` means execution stopped, including when it failed. A product requirement says `completed` means the requested goal was achieved. No decision resolving the difference exists. Draft a small vocabulary clarification and explain any required decision.
expectations: Distinguishes execution ended from goal achieved with a case where execution ends unsuccessfully.
Marks the collision unresolved, and identifies the decision needed before terms can be accepted.
Keeps current claims traceable to the two source artifacts.
negative_expectations: Must not declare either meaning accepted without a decision.
Must not silently rewrite requirements or change runtime state names.

cases.name: two-account-contexts
cases.trap: Keep domain definitions separate but invent an unsupported one-to-one relationship or shared ID across them.
cases.prompt: The Identity team calls an authenticated principal an `Account`. The Billing team calls an invoice recipient an `Account`. In one documented example, principal P1 manages billing accounts B1 and B2. Later P2 takes over B2, while B2 keeps its invoice history. No source establishes that principal IDs and billing-account IDs are shared. A colleague proposes one company-wide definition of `Account` to remove duplication. Recommend how the teams should maintain a shared vocabulary and describe the boundary between these concepts.
expectations: Identifies Identity and Billing as distinct bounded contexts and distinguishes an authenticated principal from an invoice recipient.
Preserves the documented one-to-many example (P1 manages B1 and B2) and transfer (P2 takes over B2 without changing its invoice history), without treating either as a universal relationship rule.
Describes cross-context association or translation only as supported by the examples, and marks any further relationship or ID assumptions as unresolved until evidenced.
Uses context-specific qualifiers where ambiguity matters rather than enforcing a global meaning.
negative_expectations: Must not merge authenticated principals with invoice recipients or mandate a single global meaning for Account.
Must not assert a one-to-one mapping, shared IDs, or fixed ownership as facts contrary to or unsupported by the examples.
Must not invent additional mapping rules, schemas, or product decisions to fill unknowns.

cases.name: glossary-not-breaking-rename
cases.trap: Treat a preference for a name as permission for an incompatible API and persistence migration.
cases.prompt: A team proposes the domain term `Run` instead of `Job`. Public API clients still send `jobId`, event consumers expect `JobCreated`, and persisted records contain `job_id`. The assignment is to update the glossary only. Draft the vocabulary change and identify follow-up work.
expectations: Records Run as proposed and Job as current/legacy usage, not a fully completed adoption.
Identifies the API, event, persistence, and consumer compatibility boundaries.
Limits the result to the authorized glossary scope; describes a separately reviewed migration if adoption is approved.
negative_expectations: Must not rename externally visible identifiers or persisted fields as a cosmetic cleanup.
Must not state that the new vocabulary is already implemented.

cases.name: go-style-not-domain-semantics
cases.trap: Invoke an unnecessary vocabulary process for a straightforward Go identifier convention.
cases.prompt: A Go developer asks: `Should our struct field be UserID or UserId?` There is no disagreement about what the field means. What guidance is appropriate, and does this need a domain glossary entry?
expectations: Routes to idiomatic Go naming guidance and answers the narrow naming question (UserID).
Explains why no domain-meaning clarification or glossary addition is needed.
negative_expectations: Must not invent different business concepts for ID and Id.
Must not mandate a shared-language workflow for an identifier-style question.

cases.name: accepted-meaning-vs-legacy-code
cases.trap: Mistake code terminology for intended product meaning or prematurely change storage contracts.
cases.prompt: A product owner has explicitly approved this domain distinction: `Booking` is a held reservation before payment; `Order` is a confirmed paid purchase. Existing code sometimes labels both as Order, and the task is only to draft vocabulary. Produce a compact vocabulary entry or discrepancy note.
expectations: Records the approved business distinction with source, context, status and a distinguishing example.
Reports the code's observed legacy usage separately from approved product meaning.
Flags any future renames or data changes as work requiring explicit compatibility analysis and scope.
negative_expectations: Must not infer business intent from inconsistent code labels.
Must not claim the code is already aligned or change persisted fields as part of glossary drafting.
